title: Is AI Farm Advice Accurate Enough to Trust for My Crops?
metaTitle: AI Farm Advice: How Accurate Is It, and When to Trust It
metaDescription: Is AI farm advice accurate? What AI gets right, where it fails, a five step check for any answer, and how Anee, the anee.io smart farm technician, works.
excerpt: AI farm advice is accurate enough to trust as a first opinion and a planning aid, not as the final word before you spray or spend. It is only as good as what it can see, such as a sharp photo, your crop's age, your weather and what you applied, and it slips when your field looks unlike what it learned on. On anee.io, a farm app built for Filipino farmers, Anee, its smart farm technician, uses AI and reads your own season records first. Still, confirm in the field and follow the label.

blocks.text:
Here is a real number to keep in mind. A 2016 study in Frontiers in Plant Science trained a deep learning model on leaf photos taken in a controlled setting. On test photos from that same setting, it named the crop and disease correctly 99.35 percent of the time. On photos from other sources, it got about 31 percent right. Same model, different field, very different answer.

That is the main lesson for any farmer. AI does well on questions that look like what it has seen before, and it can sound just as sure when it is wrong. So the useful question is not whether AI is accurate, but when.

items: Trust AI farm advice most for explaining, planning and reminding.
Trust it least for naming a virus or a nutrient problem from a photo alone, where look alikes are common.
Never take a spray rate or a product from AI alone. Read the label and check the FPA registration.
Give it context: crop, variety, age, place, photos and what you applied.
Check any answer with your municipal agriculturist before money changes hands.

blocks.text: Why does AI farm advice go wrong?

items: **Bad photos.** Blurry, dark or distant pictures hide the details that separate one problem from another.
**Missing context.** Without the variety, the age and the place, AI falls back on textbook answers that may not fit your field.
**Look alikes.** Tungro, nitrogen or zinc deficiency and water stress can all yellow and stunt rice.
**Different conditions.** Advice built for another country, crop or season may not fit a rainfed palay field in the Visayas.
**Confident mistakes.** A chatbot can state a wrong number in a sure voice, so every number deserves a second source.

blocks.text: How to check any AI answer in five steps

items.title: Ask for the reason
items.text: A good answer explains why and what to check. If it gives only a name or a product, ask again.

items.title: Confirm in the field
items.text: Do the check it suggests, like tapping the base of the hill or pulling a tiller.

items.title: Compare with a trusted guide
items.text: Use a farm guide you trust, such as our own [crop guides](/crops) and [pest pages](/pests).

items.title: Check the product
items.text: Look up the active ingredient in the FPA list of registered products, then follow the label for the rate.

items.title: Record what happened
items.text: Write down what you did and the result, so the next answer starts from facts.

blocks.title: Never spray on AI advice alone
blocks.text: Before you mix anything, read the product label for the crop, the pest, the rate and the days before harvest. Then check that the FPA has registered the product. That rule holds for advice from a chatbot, a neighbor or a store.

items.q: Can AI replace my agricultural technician?
items.a: Not for field visits, soil tests and lab tests, which still need people like your municipal agriculturist. For the everyday questions, though, Anee answers at any hour from your own farm's data, so you are never left guessing while you wait for the next visit.

items.q: Why does AI give different answers to the same question?
items.a: Chat tools can word things differently each time, and small changes in your question change the answer. Give the same details each time, and check numbers against a trusted source.
Some tools are free and others charge. In anee.io, the chat with Anee and her analyses use credits, on plans from PHP 70 a month, and those plans also open the Pest Finder and Disease Finder.
Yes. Anee is made for Filipino farmers and reads your own season: your lots, stages, weather and records. The app knows 85 Philippine crops, from palay and mais to vegetables and fruit trees.

items.q: What should I never let AI decide alone?
items.a: The product and the rate to spray, whether to destroy a crop, and anything that needs a signature. Those need the label, the FPA list and a person who can see your field.
